newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq resumes oil exports after six-year ban.
newsitem.headline: Iraq resumes oil exports after six-year ban.

text.p: President Saddam Hussein pressed a button that started Iraqi oil flowing to world markets on Tuesday for the first time in more than six years, the official Iraqi News Agency reported.

"President Saddam Hussein pressed the button in Kirkuk's Number One pumping station at 11.25 Baghdad time (0825 GMT), declaring the return of Iraqi oil to the international market," the agency reported from Kirkuk in northern Iraq.
Shortly afterward, Turkey's state-owned refiner Tupras said it had signed a contract with Iraq to buy 75,000 barrels per day (bpd) of the new exports.

Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said in a statement Iraq would pump 650,000 barrels on Tuesday from Kirkuk through a pipeline across Turkey. He said Iraq would give preference to Turkey in selling its oil.

The United Nations gave Iraq clearance on Monday for limited exports from Tuesday under an "oil-for-food" deal to buy humanitarian aid for Iraqis suffering under economic sanctions imposed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
Iraqis celebrated in the streets of Baghdad on Monday night, firing in the air and singing and dancing, residents said.
"Iraq will export today (Tuesday) 650,000 barrels of crude oil through the Turkish terminal of Ceyhan," Rasheed said in a statement carried by the official Iraqi News Agency.

World crude oil prices opened slightly lower. Benchmark Brent Blend crude from the North Sea for January delivery began the morning 18 cents below Monday's close and later fell a further 10 cents to $23.84 a barrel at 1035 GMT.

"The response has been muted," said Alistair Harris, energy manager at Mees Pierson brokerage in London. "We are a little sceptical of downside action and we noticed the lack of weakness on Monday of the U.S. market."
A spokesman for Turkey's energy ministry said a celebration to mark the loading of tankers in Ceyhan would likely take place December 16.
Oil from Iraq's southern terminal of Mina al-Bakr would start to flow on Friday or Saturday, Rasheed added. Under the U.N. deal, the majority of exports must be via Turkey.

But oil industry sources in Asia said on Tuesday Iraqi crude oil was unlikely to hit Asia until January due to problems at Mina al-Bakr and the reluctance of regional refiners to lift the crude at such short notice.

"The lines and equipment at the terminal are not totally acceptable. Some of the pipelines have rusted and corroded and need to be replaced," said a source close to the U.N.-appointed inspectorate from the Dutch-based Saybolt company.
Under the U.N. plan, drawn up in May but delayed by disputes over implementation, Iraq can sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian goods.
Security Council President Francesco Paolo Fulci of Italy called it "the largest humanitarian operation ever launched by the United Nations."

Speaking in New York after notifying council members that Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali had given the go-ahead, Fulci said: "More than 20 million innocent Iraqi civilians will be finally saved from starvation and untold suffering."
Both oil sales and the purchase of humanitarian supplies are subject to close U.N. monitoring. If all goes well, the Security Council may renew the deal when the initial six months expire.

However, in Washington State Department deputy spokesman Glyn Davies stressed the agreement did "not signal an end or the first step toward the end of the sanctions regime against Iraq, against (President) Saddam Hussein's regime."
A key condition for ending sanctions, which ban normal oil sales, is verification from a U.N. Special Commission that all Iraq's weapons of mass destruction have been scrapped.
The head of the commission, ambassador Rolf Ekeus, was in Bagdad as the oil exports began, trying to account for Iraq's arsenal of Scud missiles.
Traders and shipping sources said in Europe on Monday it was highly unlikely Iraqi oil would hit the market for at least a couple of weeks.
Spokesmen for France's Elf Aquitaine and Total, two of the first companies expected to conclude contracts, said on Monday their firms had not signed deals yet.

In giving the green light, Boutros-Ghali said: "This is a victory for the poorest of the poor of Iraq, for the women, the children, the sick and the disabled." The U.N. World Food Programme estimated about 180,000 children under five were malnourished.
